overview: Medieval Norway developed through a long process of political consolidation, rather than a single securely dated founding. Timber churches, waterfront buildings, inscribed sticks and legal manuscripts show how people built, traded and communicated. Later royal unions changed the kingdom's independence; they did not end Norwegian communities or their accumulated knowledge.

periods.title: Coastal power and gradual consolidation
periods.summary: Harald Fairhair's power was centred in southwestern Norway and connected with coastal trade. Accounts presenting him as ruler of a fully unified country took shape later. Consolidation continued through subsequent rulers.

periods.title: Churches and trading towns
periods.summary: Carpenters built and altered stave churches while Bergen grew as a trading centre. Buildings and waterfront plots preserve evidence of construction, storage and commerce through successive rebuilding.

periods.title: A common legal framework
periods.summary: Magnus VI's National Law of 1274 brought regional assembly traditions into a common framework. Its handwritten copies preserve differences in how scribes transmitted sensitive provisions.

periods.title: A shared ruler with Denmark
periods.summary: Norway and Denmark came under a shared ruler in 1380. Norway remained a distinct realm with its own council within this dynastic arrangement.

periods.title: Norway within the Scandinavian union
periods.summary: Erik's coronation in 1397 joined three Scandinavian crowns. Norway retained distinct institutions within the union, although its political autonomy became increasingly constrained.

periods.title: Subordination and religious change
periods.summary: Christian III's intervention ended the old council's effective role and dismantled the Catholic church province. Lutheran institutions developed under royal authority, while religious change among the wider population took longer.

items.text: Urnes Stave Church translates a basilica layout into timber. Columns, arches, roof framing and shingles worked together to create a substantial interior. The building shows carpenters adapting an architectural language familiar from stone churches to a different material.

Urnes reuses carved elements from an eleventh-century predecessor, including interlaced animals on the north wall. Older craft remained visible within a later Christian building. Reuse means the date of a carving and the date of its present setting can differ.

The surviving church rests on a sill frame above stone foundations, unlike an earlier structure with posts set into the ground. Medieval furnishings and later alterations also survive. The site records successive solutions to building and worship, rather than one unchanging moment.

Bergen connected northern Norwegian stockfish producers with wider markets. Hanseatic merchants gained royal trading privileges and developed a permanent presence at Bryggen. The trade joined fishing and preservation to transport, storage and negotiation over access to markets.

Bryggen's narrow plots placed homes and offices near the harbour, warehouses farther back, and communal rooms and kitchens behind them. Stone storerooms protected valuable goods from fire. This arrangement made the waterfront both a workplace and a setting for communal living.

Repeated fires destroyed Bryggen's buildings, which were rebuilt on earlier plots using traditional techniques. Much of today's appearance follows the fire of 1702. A medieval plan can survive through replacement buildings, so the standing timber should not all be dated to the Middle Ages.

A thirteenth-century tally stick from Bugarden at Bryggen carries counting notches on one side and an affectionate runic message on another. Catalogued as B118, it brings commercial record-keeping and personal communication together on a small wooden object.

Another Bugarden stick, dated to the middle decades of the thirteenth century, combines an affectionate request with the opening letters of the runic alphabet. The alphabet could have carried magical meaning, but its precise use remains an interpretation, not a directly observed ritual.

Magnus VI introduced the National Law in 1274, bringing regional assembly traditions into a kingdom-wide legal framework. Surviving handwritten copies preserve the work of scribes as well as legislators. A separate City Law followed in 1276, reflecting distinct needs of urban communities.

Copies of the National Law disagree over retaliation and other sensitive rules, including poor relief and women's rights. Those variations make the manuscripts evidence of contested legal change. The text of a royal law does not demonstrate that every court or household followed it uniformly.

Erik's coronation at Kalmar in 1397 brought Norway, Denmark and Sweden under a shared monarch. Historians still debate parts of the agreement's legal meaning. Sharing a king was not initially the same as abolishing each realm's council and separate political identity.

The Reformation imposed in 1536 and 1537 replaced medieval church arrangements with Lutheran institutions under the king. The Church of Norway's history distinguishes that official change from its slower reception among ordinary people. Government decisions and lived religious practice followed different timelines.

ending.text: Royal military intervention in 1537, following Christian III's commitments in 1536, sharply reduced Norway's autonomy and ended its medieval council and Catholic church province. Norway remained a recognisable kingdom within a Danish-centred monarchy, with continuing communities and local administration. The map endpoint of 1400 does not mark this transition or a cultural extinction.

sources.title: Store norske leksikon, Harald Harfagre
sources.note: Opening discussion: approximate ninth- and tenth-century kingship, southwestern core, coastal trade and later construction of the unification narrative. The traditional 872 date is not treated as a verified national founding.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Urnes Stave Church
sources.note: Brief synthesis, Integrity and Authenticity: timber basilica, older reused carving, sill frame on stone foundations, medieval furnishings and later alterations.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Bryggen
sources.note: Brief synthesis and Integrity: stockfish trade, royal privileges, narrow plots, warehouses and kitchen facilities; present appearance chiefly follows reconstruction after the 1702 fire.

sources.title: Gitte Hansen, Runic sticks from Bergen, University Museum of Bergen
sources.note: Bugarden section, tally stick B118 (BRM 0/17540), dated 1225/30-1248; stick with affectionate text and futhark, dated 1250-1275. Magical use is proposed, not established; find contexts are thirteenth-century urban deposits.

sources.title: National Library of Norway, National Law anniversary
sources.note: What is the National Law of 1274? and exhibition account: Magnus VI, regional assembly traditions and surviving manuscripts. Broad claims of European priority or modern democracy are not adopted.

sources.title: Norwegian Parliament, The Landslov of 1274
sources.note: The Landslov and European legislation: scribal variation in retaliation, poor relief and women's rights; separate City Law of 1276. Legal prescriptions are not proof of universal compliance.

sources.title: Store norske leksikon, Norway in the late Middle Ages
sources.note: Fra innenlandsk til unionelt kongedomme: 1380 succession, 1397 coronation and debated union terms; opening discussion distinguishes subordination in 1537 from disappearance of Norway as a named kingdom.

sources.title: Tor Ragnar Weidling and Magne Njastad, Norway under Danish rule, Store norske leksikon
sources.note: Lydriketiden 1537-1660: royal commitment in 1536, military action and institutional changes in 1537, and limited rather than complete incorporation. Later local administration and economic activity show continuity.

sources.title: Church of Norway, history of the church
sources.note: Reformation section: introduction in 1536-1537, official Lutheran religion, replacement of medieval ecclesiastical arrangements and gradual reception among the population.
